title: Request validation

richText: Bean Validation checks Java data against declared rules called constraints.
Put request constraints on a request DTO so they match the data the client can send.
Add spring-boot-starter-validation to supply the validation implementation.
Spring Boot 3 and later use jakarta.validation imports. Older Boot 2 examples use javax.validation.
Validation checks the rules you declare. It does not check permissions or replace database constraints.

1: The value must not be null. An empty String still passes.
A String must contain a non-whitespace character.
A String, collection, map or array must be non-null and non-empty.
The length or size must be within the limits. Null passes.
A String must satisfy the validator’s email-format rule. Null passes.
A supported numeric value must be within the limit.

richText: Combine constraints when needed. @Email alone does not require a value.
Choose a constraint for the field type. @NotEmpty does not apply to int; use a numeric constraint.
@Valid on a @RequestBody argument checks the converted DTO before the handler runs.
For this argument validation, failed constraints normally raise MethodArgumentNotValidException and produce HTTP 400.
The default response body depends on configuration. Do not assume it includes every constraint message.
@Valid on a nested DTO field also requests validation of that nested object.

example.title: Reject a blank name or invalid email
description: Use spring-boot-starter-validation and Java 17 or later in a Spring Boot 3+ MVC application.
Place these types in separate files. Send JSON to POST /users/check.
explanation: @NotBlank rejects a missing, empty or whitespace-only username and email.
@Size restricts the username length. @Email checks the email format.
A body such as {"username":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"} reaches the method and is returned.
A body with username set to "" fails validation before check() runs. The default status is 400.
This endpoint checks and echoes data. It does not create a user.

richText: Use exception advice to translate validation errors into the API’s error response format.
To handle errors inside the controller, place Errors or BindingResult immediately after the validated argument. Check it before processing the input.
For a rule the built-in constraints cannot express, define a constraint annotation with @Constraint and a ConstraintValidator.
In Spring MVC 6.1 and later, direct constraints on handler parameters can use method validation and raise HandlerMethodValidationException. This differs from validating one request DTO.

summary: Declare input rules, run them with @Valid and handle failures.
